chunks: "The components that drive the layer count up are the ones that are dense, fast, or have lots of supplies. Fine-pitch BGAs are the main one.
With a BGA you have to bring every signal out from under the chip, and once the pitch is 0.
8 mm or less you can only fit one trace between pads, so you get roughly two rows of balls per layer. A few hundred balls can need four or more signal layers just for escape.
FPGAs and application processors are the standard examples, and that's why they're usually six to ten layers.
Then there are fast interfaces: DDR memory, PCIe, USB 3, HDMI, gigabit Ethernet.
They need controlled impedance, a solid reference plane beside every routing layer, and tight length matching, so you add layers to give each signal layer its own plane.
Third is power: a processor with a core rail, an I/O rail, DDR, analog and so on needs several planes or islands and lots of decoupling, and that adds power layers.
And RF or mixed-signal parts need isolation and clean ground planes, so you put those on dedicated layers. Big connectors or backplanes with hundreds of pins also drive layers.
Simple parts like small QFP microcontrollers, op-amps and power regulators don't, which is why a hobby board can be two layers."
